entities.name: Alisher Navoi State Museum of Literature
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Alisher Navoi State Museum of Literature (Uzbek: Alisher Navoiy nomidagi O'zbekiston davlat adabiyot muzeyi) in Tashkent, Uzbekistan — named for Alisher Navoi (1441-1501), the 15th-century Chagatai poet considered the father of Uzbek literature and one of the greatest literary figures in the Islamic literary tradition — is Uzbekistan's primary literary museum, housing manuscripts, documents, and materials related to Navoi and the broader history of Uzbek and Central Asian literature.

Alisher Navoi is one of the towering figures of Islamic literary history: writing in Chagatai Turkish (the literary language of Central Asia that is the ancestor of modern Uzbek), he produced extraordinary poetry (especially his Khamsa, five allegorical masnavi poems responding to Nizami Ganjavi's classical Khamsa), prose works, and a foundational comparative linguistic treatise (Muhakamat al-lughatayn, comparing Chagatai Turkish and Persian). He served as a vizier to the Timurid Sultan Husayn Bayqara in Herat and was central to the last great flowering of Timurid culture.

Navoi's significance extends beyond literature: he championed the use of Chagatai Turkish as a literary language worthy of comparison with Persian (the dominant literary language of the Islamic world), legitimizing Turkic literary culture at a time when Persian was considered culturally superior. His works became the foundation of Uzbek literary identity, and Soviet cultural policy used Navoi as a national symbol of Uzbek cultural heritage — naming the national opera theater and major institutions after him. The museum bearing his name serves as the primary institutional guardian of Uzbek literary heritage.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Alisher Navoi State Museum of Literature — dedicated to the father of Uzbek literature who championed Chagatai Turkish against Persian cultural dominance and produced the Timurid era's greatest literary works — is historically significant as the primary guardian of Central Asian Turkic literary heritage.
